answer:
The century in which Pottery Form diversity collapsed while Pottery Decoration diversity increased simultaneously is the 18th century BCE (circa 1700 BCE). At the 100-year data point labeled 1700 BCE, pottery-form diversity (ZKeform) collapsed from +0.74 (1800 BCE) by −1.87 z-units to its sustained global minimum of −1.13, and in that same century pottery-decoration diversity (Zkeverz) rose from −0.48 (1800 BCE) by +1.45 z-units to a sustained elevated plateau of +0.97 (later rising further to +1.53 by the 11th century BCE). Change-point analysis finds a structural break entering 1700 BCE in BOTH series (stable across penalties 3–8 for form; penalties ≥6 for decoration), and this century is unique — no other century satisfies both onset conditions under the approved operationalization. Boundary note: the transition occurs between the BCE-1800 (19th century BCE) and BCE-1700 (18th century BCE) data points; the first century in which both conditions are jointly recorded is the 18th century BCE (span 1800–1701 BCE).

Sensitivity flag (reported honestly, per the approved rules): the answer holds under the regime-onset operationalization — Form collapse = onset of the sustained global-minimum regime (−1.13) with a preceding single-step drop ≥ 1.5 z-units; Decoration increase = onset of a sustained elevated regime (≥ +0.9 held ≥ 3 consecutive centuries). If instead "decoration increase" were anchored to its later global maximum (+1.53 at BCE 1000) or to a mean+1SD threshold (z > 1.00, first met at BCE 1000), then NO single century would satisfy both a form-collapse onset and a decoration-increase onset, contradicting the question's simultaneity premise. The only other large decoration step (+1.81 at BCE 4000) is a one-time recovery from the series-start trough, immediately followed by ~30 centuries of low values, so it is not an increase; likewise the form's −1.13 value at the series start (BCE 4300–4100) has no preceding step-drop and is a start-of-series artifact, not a collapse.

payload.hypothesis: Pottery Form diversity collapsed and Pottery Decoration diversity increased simultaneously in the 18th century BCE (circa 1700 BCE): at the 1700 BCE data point form diversity fell to its sustained global minimum −1.13 (step −1.87 from +0.74) while decoration diversity rose to a sustained +0.97 plateau (step +1.45 from −0.48, later reaching +1.53 by the 11th century BCE); change-point detection flags both breaks entering 1700 BCE and no other century satisfies both onset conditions.
payload.workflow: 1) Load capital.csv (decimal-comma parsing) and time_series_data.csv; validate the two pottery series are identical on shared centuries (0 mismatches). 2) Primary rules on the decadal series: Form collapse onset = first century at sustained global min (−1.13) with preceding step drop ≥1.5 → 1700 BCE; Decoration increase onset = first century with sustained z ≥ 0.9 (≥3 consecutive centuries) → 1700 BCE; intersection = {1700}. 3) Uniqueness enumeration confirms only BCE 1700. 4) Cross-check with exact penalized-DP (PELT/L2) change-point detection on both series: stable break entering BCE 1700 in both. 5) Sensitivity analysis: stricter decoration thresholds (mean+1SD or global-max anchoring) shift decoration onset to BCE 1000, giving no simultaneous century — flagged. 6) Century naming: BCE-1700 data point → 18th century BCE (1800–1701 BCE), boundary between 19th/18th centuries BCE noted.
